This is Punjab, the land of five rivers. And its water account is in the red.
Every year, rain and rivers let Punjab safely draw about 16.8 billion cubic metres of groundwater. It draws 26.3.
That's 156 percent of what it can safely take. The highest of any state.
NASA's GRACE satellites saw it from orbit. Between 2002 and 2008, north-west India lost 109 cubic kilometres of groundwater.
Most of it goes on one crop. A kilo of paddy can take around 3,000 litres of water.
So why keep withdrawing? Since 1997, power for farm pumps has been free. And the government buys almost every grain of paddy at a fixed price.
For a farmer, it's the safest bet. Maize often sells below its support price. Paddy doesn't.
The overdraft is shrinking, slowly. From 164 percent in 2023, to 156 now, as canals water more fields.
But a 2019 draft government report warned Punjab could turn into a desert within 25 years at this pace.
For decades, the water sat about half a metre deeper every year. Every new pump has to dig further.
A bank lets you run an overdraft. An aquifer doesn't. So what should Punjab grow instead?
